newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Violence-ravaged Albania set for vital election.
newsitem.headline: Violence-ravaged Albania set for vital election.

text.p: Elections aimed at preventing Albania reverting to chaos were back on course on Thursday as the country's second-largest party agreed to take part in the vote.

Agreement by the Socialist Party to run in the June 29 election, provided there is full monitoring by the international community, ends months of deadlock and lifted a last obstacle to the ballot going ahead.

"We took a political decision which represents a responsible attitude of the Socialist Party to take part only in guaranteed free, democratic and fair elections," Socialist Party chairman Fatos Nano told reporters.
"The Socialist Party will only take part in elections that have an international guarantee they will be free, fair and equal," the party said in a statement.
Other parties in Prime Minister Bashkim Fino's nine-party government have not yet said whether they will taske part in the vote.
However, European envoy Franz Vranitzky said in Vienna earlier that Fino had called him the previous night and assured him the parties had agreed to participate.
Albania needs the election to restore law and order after unrest in March sparked by the collapse of shady investment schemes that left many penniless in Europe's poorest country.
The Socialists and other parties had refused to stand over electoral rules they said were tilted in favour of right-wing President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.
The Socialists, reformed heirs of the Communist Party that ruled this mountainous state with an iron fist for more than 40 years, are the main rivals to the Democratic Party.
Berisha meanwhile kept on with his electoral campaign, visiting the town of Elbasan, 54 km (30 miles) from Tirana, attacking the Socialists and promising to overcome the chaos.

"We are determined to set forward an emergency programme to overcome the crisis. It is more suitable and the best one for Albania's integration into Europe and the consolidation of an advanced Western democracy," he told around 1,500 supporters.
"The socialism of the communists is dictatorship," he said.

Fino, a Socialist leading a national unity government installed as the riots reached a peak, asked the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on Wednesday for "Bosnia-style" monitoring.
The Socialists pulled out of elections in May 1996, saying they were rigged. The OSCE called those elections seriously flawed.
The Socialists said they wanted the OSCE, the Council of Europe and the European Union to be involved at every step of the coming election right up the final count.
Vranitsky, special OSCE envoy to Albania, earlier reassured the Balkan nation of support for the election and said that as many observers as necessary would be sent.

"We will help Albania. The whole international community is speaking with unanimity. There are no dissenting voices," he told a news conference after addressing the OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council.
One politician said Albania needed the same kind of all-embracing monitoring of its election as in Bosnia.
Albania is much calmer than at the height of the violence in March, but several regions are still tense and large swathes of the country are without any state control.
Gangs armed during the wholesale looting of army barracks, when around one million weapons fell into civilian hands, appear to roam free and police are absent from many areas.
